caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:000978
attempts.entry_title: Geometry of PFC and CA1 spatial codes during W-track learning (Wakhloo, Slatton and Chung 2026)
attempts.summary: In these rat PFC and CA1 recordings, the paper's learning results held up: behavioural and readout errors fell over four sessions then plateaued, the theory tracked the measured readout error, and total dimension fell early while task-relevant dimension and nearly every other geometric measure rose. The late match to optimal codes held in PFC but not in CA1, where task-relevant dimension fell after session four on the code's 19-unit subsets. The linear SSF trend in CA1 just missed its bound with the Methods' 24 units but held with the code's 19. The theory, network simulations and macaque analyses could not be tested, as their data are not in this dataset.
attempts.description: Tests the rat findings of Wakhloo, Slatton and Chung (2026) on dandiset 000978, which holds the spikes, position and trials of 8 rats learning a W-track alternation task over 8 sessions in one day. It computes the task-averaged readout error of position and velocity, its geometric terms and the GLM task-relevant dimension per rat and session, with the paper's mixed-effects models. The paper's theory, network simulations and macaque and pose analyses are not about this dataset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Wakhloo, Slatton and Chung (2026) from dandiset 000978

outcomes.statement: Under a Gaussian approximation, the task-averaged generalization error of a Hebbian linear readout is a strictly decreasing function of four geometric terms of the population activity (neural-latent correlation c, signal-signal factorization f, signal-noise factorization s and the participation ratio of the responses) and of the number of training samples p (Eq. 1).
outcomes.source: Results, Geometric measures govern generalization of linear readouts, paragraph 3; Methods, Decomposition of generalization error across tasks
outcomes.quote: we prove that, under a certain Gaussian approximation, the error E g is given by ... where we have written the generalization error as a strictly decreasing function of four geometric terms as well as the number of samples in the training dataset, p
outcomes.notes: A theoretical result, proved in Supplementary Information section 1; no recorded data test it. Its rat counterpart is tested in fig7f-theory-vs-empirical.

outcomes.statement: The error contributions of the neural dimension and the neural-latent correlation vanish as the number of training samples grows, while the contributions of the two factorization terms are an irreducible error independent of the sample size.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometric measures govern generalization of linear readouts, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: the contribution to the error of the neural dimension and neural–latent correlation decays to zero with the number of training samples ... the error stemming from the SSF and SNF represents an ‘irreducible error’ that does not depend on the number of training samples
outcomes.notes: A property of the form of Eq. 1; no recorded data test it.

outcomes.statement: In random and trained multilayer perceptrons fed Gaussian latents, the theoretical error of Eq. 1 closely tracks the empirical Hebbian readout error across layers, and the trained network reaches a lower error in its later layers.
outcomes.source: Figure 3b,c and legend; Results, Geometry of multitask learning in multilayer perceptrons, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Theoretical predictions closely track empirical errors, and the trained network achieves a lower error in later layers
outcomes.notes: A simulation of multilayer perceptrons (code/run_mlp_exps.py), not a finding on recorded data; the dataset cannot test it, and it was not run here.

outcomes.statement: In the trained MLP, each ReLU raises the neural dimension at the cost of the correlation, each linear layer raises the correlation while the dimension falls, and SSF and SNF increase monotonically through the penultimate layer; the random network does not show this pattern.
outcomes.source: Figure 3d-g and legend; Results, Geometry of multitask learning in multilayer perceptrons, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: the neural dimension spikes each time the nonlinearity is applied, at the cost of the total correlation ... both the SSF and SNF terms monotonically increase through the penultimate layer of the network. Notably, this pattern is not present in the random network
outcomes.notes: A simulation of multilayer perceptrons, not a finding on recorded data; not run here.

outcomes.statement: Across the layers of a DeepLabCut ResNet50 pose estimation network, with the 24 marker coordinates of an adult mouse as latents, the dimension increases, the neural-latent correlation decays, SSF and SNF improve monotonically and the multitask error decreases.
outcomes.source: Figure 4b-f legend; Results, Disentangling in deep pose estimation networks, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The total dimensionality of the DCNN’s intermediate representations increases across layers ... The total correlation between the latents and the network’s internal representations decays across layers ... Both SSF and SNF improve monotonically across layers ... Multitask error decreases across layers
outcomes.notes: The data are the DeepLabCut parenting mouse benchmark, outside the dataset. Testing the claim needs a ResNet50 pose network trained as in the Methods; the paper's code README says the training "can take a few hours" and "must be executed in a separate Python 3.8 virtual environment" (code/setup_deeplabcut.py), which an entry locked to Python 3.13 cannot install, and which does not fit the run's time. Not attempted.
outcomes.where: DeepLabCut parenting mouse benchmark dataset (github.com/DeepLabCut/DeepLabCut), with a network trained as in Methods, Analysis of pose estimation network

outcomes.statement: For the pose estimation network, the theoretical error is biased but linearly explains practically all the variance of the empirical multitask error across layers (R2 = 0.988).
outcomes.source: Figure 4g; Results, Disentangling in deep pose estimation networks, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: the analytical prediction for E g still linearly explains practically all of the variance in the empirically computed multitask error ( R 2 = 0.988)
outcomes.notes: Needs the trained pose network of fig4bf-pose-network-geometry; not attempted.

outcomes.statement: For macaque V4 and IT responses and raw pixels, Eq. 1 accurately predicts the Hebbian readout error, best for the neural responses, and the error improves through the ventral stream.
outcomes.source: Figure 5d; Results, Predicting readout performance of macaque visual representations, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: We find that our formula accurately predicts the generalization error, particularly for the neural response readouts (Fig. 5d ). Furthermore, we find that generalization error improves through the ventral stream
outcomes.notes: The data are the Majaj et al. (2015) V4 and IT responses via Brain-Score, outside the dataset and public. Not attempted in this run, whose five hours went to the rat claims; a later attempt can test it.
outcomes.where: Majaj et al. 2015 V4 and IT data via Brain-Score (github.com/brain-score/vision)

outcomes.statement: The dimension is lower in V4 than in IT or the pixels, and the neural-latent correlation increases from the pixels to the visual areas.
outcomes.source: Figure 5e-h legend; Results, Predicting readout performance of macaque visual representations, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: we find that the dimension is lower in V4 than in either IT or the pixel data 24 (Fig. 5e ) and that the correlation increases from the pixels to the visual areas

statistics.test: two-sided paired t-test across object categories

outcomes.notes: Brain-Score data outside the dataset; not attempted in this run (see fig5d).
outcomes.where: Majaj et al. 2015 V4 and IT data via Brain-Score (github.com/brain-score/vision)

outcomes.statement: The most marked factorization trend is an increase of the signal-noise factorization in IT, so that latent-unrelated variability overlaps less with the coding directions in IT than in V4 or the pixels.
outcomes.source: Figure 5e-h legend; Results, Predicting readout performance of macaque visual representations, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Turning to the factorization measures, the most dramatic trend is the increase in SNF in IT

statistics.test: two-sided paired t-test across object categories

outcomes.notes: Brain-Score data outside the dataset; not attempted in this run (see fig5d).
outcomes.where: Majaj et al. 2015 V4 and IT data via Brain-Score (github.com/brain-score/vision)

outcomes.statement: The representation that minimizes the error disentangles the latents; with uncorrelated latents, distinct latents lie along orthogonal neural directions, and with correlated latents the principal components of the latents map onto those of the neural activity.
outcomes.source: Results, Optimal representation of latent variables, paragraph 2; Methods, Optimal codes
outcomes.quote: We show analytically that the optimal representation disentangles latent variables
outcomes.notes: A theoretical result (Supplementary Information section 4); no recorded data test it.

outcomes.statement: The optimal code's covariance has eigenvalues psi_i proportional to omega_i / (2 p omega_i + pi sum_k omega_k) (Eq. 2), so its spectrum flattens as the number of training samples grows, giving more variance to less informative latents.
outcomes.source: Results, Optimal representation of latent variables, paragraph 3; Figure 6b; Methods, Optimal codes
outcomes.quote: we show that the optimal code’s covariance matrix has at least d non-zero eigenvalues that are given by ... We can see that, as p grows, the spectrum becomes increasingly flat, reflecting the expansion strategy
outcomes.notes: A theoretical result checked by numerical optimisation; no recorded data test it.

outcomes.statement: Early in learning (small p), optimal codes have a higher neural-latent correlation and a lower dimension and SSF than late in learning.
outcomes.source: Figure 6c-e legend; Results, Optimal representation of latent variables, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Early in training, optimal representations have a higher neural–latent correlation and a lower dimension and SSF than they do late in training
outcomes.notes: A theoretical prediction; no recorded data test it. Its rat counterpart is late-trends-match-optimal.

outcomes.statement: Across every analysis of the paper, the Hebbian readout error is strongly correlated with the empirical error of a linear support vector classifier trained on the same tasks, particularly in the brain data.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 3; Supplementary Fig. 3 (not in the text read)
outcomes.quote: Across every analysis reported in this paper, we found a strong correlation between SVC and Hebbian errors, particularly in the brain data
outcomes.notes: Only the PFC and CA1 part is tested. Over the 64 rat and session values the squared Pearson correlation between the theoretical Hebbian error and the linear SVC error is 0.926 in PFC and 0.832 in CA1 (P below 1e-24), so readings (a) and (b) both hold in both areas. With the empirical Hebbian error (variant) it is 0.943 and 0.946. SVC errors run from 0.197 to 0.362 (PFC) and 0.200 to 0.360 (CA1). The rest of the statement (MLPs, macaque, pose network) is not tested. The SVC is trained and tested on bins drawn at random from 500 ms bins that are correlated in time, as in the paper's code, so its errors are likely optimistic in absolute value; the criterion is a correlation over sessions.
deviations: The SVC is fitted on 4 of the 500 subsets per session (every 125th), as one per task on all 500 would take about 25 hours on one core; the theoretical error is the mean over all 500. On the same 4 subsets the theoretical error gives r2 = 0.931 (PFC) and 0.829 (CA1).
CA1 uses 24 units per subset (Methods); the paper's SVC figure used 19.

outcomes.statement: Behavioural error on the continuous alternation task decreases quickly over the first few sessions and largely plateaus after session four.
outcomes.source: Figure 7d legend; Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Behavioral error on the continuous alternation task and neural readout error quickly decrease over the first few sessions ... After session four, both behavioral and readout error largely plateau
outcomes.notes: Mean behavioural error over the 8 rats is 0.668 at session 1, 0.157 at session 4 and 0.180 at session 8; the drop from 1 to 4 (0.511) is larger than the change from 4 to 8 (0.023), and session 4 is lower than session 1 in 8 of 8 rats. The linear mixed model over sessions 1 to 4 has a slope of -0.166 per session (P = 5.8e-18). The per-rat values equal those of the paper's results file (largest difference 1e-14).

outcomes.statement: The task-averaged neural readout error for position and velocity, in PFC and in CA1, decreases over learning, quickly over the first few sessions, then largely plateaus after session four.
outcomes.source: Figure 7e legend; Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraphs 1 and 2
outcomes.quote: These readout errors decrease over learning (Fig. 7e,f )
outcomes.notes: Theoretical error (main reading), mean over rats, PFC 0.3626, 0.3167 and 0.3320 at sessions 1, 4 and 8 (drop 0.0459, change after session 4 0.0153); CA1 0.3523, 0.3121 and 0.3241 (0.0401, 0.0119). The criterion holds in both areas under both readings (empirical Hebbian error, PFC drop 0.0733 and change 0.0313) and with 19 CA1 units. Both areas rise again at session 8. The empirical Hebbian error is trained and tested on bins drawn at random from 500 ms bins that are correlated in time, as in the paper's code (utils.emp_error), so it is likely optimistic in absolute value; the criterion compares sessions, not absolute values.
deviations: The random subsets use this attempt's seeds; the per-session means agree with the paper's file to a median relative difference of 0.14% (PFC theory).

outcomes.statement: Single-session readout errors correlate with behavioural task error, with R2 = 0.48 in CA1 and 0.51 in PFC.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 1; Figure 7d,e legend; Supplementary Fig. 12c (not read)
outcomes.quote: are correlated with single-session behavioral task performance ( R 2 = 0.48 (CA1) and R 2 = 0.51 (PFC); Supplementary Fig. 12c )
outcomes.notes: Squared correlation over the 64 points between behavioural error and theoretical error, CA1 0.493 and PFC 0.508 (P = 1.0e-10 and 4.0e-11), both within tolerance. With the empirical Hebbian error CA1 is 0.579 (outside) and PFC 0.536. With the code's 19 CA1 units the theoretical reading gives 0.475, and the paper's results file gives 0.477 and 0.510. Per rat the r2 ranges from 0.111 (JS34, CA1) to 0.979 (JS21, PFC).

outcomes.statement: The theoretical readout error of Eq. 1 agrees well overall with the empirical Hebbian readout error over rat sessions in PFC and CA1, with a small bias at low error values.
outcomes.source: Figure 7f legend
outcomes.quote: Empirical generalization error versus our estimate from equation ( 1 ). Although there is a small bias for low error values, we find a good agreement overall
outcomes.notes: The theoretical and empirical errors correlate with r = 0.983 in PFC (P = 2.5e-47) and 0.948 in CA1 with 24 units (P = 1.9e-32), both above the criterion's 0.9; with the code's 19 CA1 units r = 0.960. The paper's results file gives 0.982 and 0.960 (19 units). Reported and not judged, the theory lies above the empirical error by a mean of 0.0341 (PFC) and 0.0311 (CA1), by 0.048 and 0.044 in the lowest-error quarter and 0.015 and 0.016 in the highest, the bias at low error the legend describes; the mean absolute difference is 11.55% (PFC) and 10.69% (CA1, 24 units) of the mean empirical error. Like for like with the paper's file, which uses 19 CA1 units, it is 11.55% against 11.55% in PFC and 8.91% against 9.04% in CA1. What the answer changed. This attempt asked whether the criterion's bound of a mean absolute difference below 10% of the mean empirical error misread the legend, since the paper's own results fail it in PFC. The reader agreed and amended the criterion to a positive Pearson correlation with p < 0.05 and r of at least 0.9 in each area, with the differences reported and not judged (questions/wakhloo-2026.yaml, answered 2026-11-10). Under the earlier criterion the outcome was not_reproduced (PFC 11.55% and CA1 10.69% above the bound); under the amended one, re-run here on the same numbers, both areas hold and the claim is reproduced. The 300 training and 200 test bins are drawn at random from 500 ms bins that are correlated in time, and the units are normalised over all bins, as in the paper's code (utils.emp_error), so the empirical errors here and in the paper are likely optimistic. This bears on the size of the gap between theory and empirical error, which is reported and not judged, not on the correlation.

outcomes.statement: The total neural dimension in PFC and CA1 drops over the first four sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Figure 7g; Methods, Generalized linear model analysis, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Interestingly, we find that although the total neural dimension drops over these initial sessions (Fig. 7g )
outcomes.notes: Mean total dimension, session 1 to 4, PFC 15.833 to 14.516 and CA1 19.537 to 18.130 (19 units, 16.027 to 15.128), lower at session 4 in 8 of 8 rats in each area; mixed slopes over sessions 1 to 4 of -0.426 (P = 1.3e-14) and -0.485 (P = 3.5e-08).

outcomes.statement: The dimension of the subspace holding task-relevant variability, estimated from Poisson GLMs, increases over learning, including over the first four sessions in which the total dimension falls.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Figure 7h; Methods, Generalized linear model analysis, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: the dimension of the subspace containing task-relevant information (that is, the dimension of the ‘signal subspace’) increases monotonically over learning, even during those initial four sessions (Fig. 7h )
outcomes.notes: Reading (a) holds in both areas; mean task-relevant dimension at sessions 1, 4 and 8, PFC 7.131, 9.040 and 9.543, CA1 6.892, 9.134 and 9.008 (19 units, as the code), higher at session 4 in 7 of 8 PFC and 8 of 8 CA1 rats. Reading (b) fails in both areas; the PFC mean falls from session 6 to 7 (9.322 to 9.238) and the CA1 mean from 5 to 6 and from 7 to 8 (9.497 to 9.008). With 24 CA1 units the means are 7.926, 10.286 and 10.260. Units replaced by the null model are 334 of 2327 in PFC and 685 of 3357 in CA1.
deviations: The GLM basis is the one the code chose (position bins 10 cm, velocity bins 3 cm/s, variances 100 and 40); its grid search over 108 basis settings was not repeated, as each setting costs about 27 minutes here.

outcomes.statement: Over the first four sessions, nearly every geometric measure (task-relevant dimension, SSF, neural-latent correlation and SNF) increases in PFC and CA1.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Figure 7h-k
outcomes.quote: Over the first four sessions, both behavioral and neural readout error rapidly improve (Fig. 7d,e ). During this time, nearly every geometric measure increases (Fig. 7h–k )
outcomes.notes: From session 1 to 4 all four measures increase in PFC (task dimension 7.131 to 9.040, SSF 0.6323 to 0.6661, correlation 0.0182 to 0.0337, SNF 0.3426 to 0.6985); in CA1 three of four do, SSF falling from 0.6905 to 0.6787. The task dimension is on 19-unit subsets, as the claims file's pipeline takes it. The 19-unit CA1 variant gives the same three, and so does CA1 with the task dimension on 24-unit subsets (7.926 to 10.286).

outcomes.statement: After session four, several early trends reverse; the total dimension begins to increase while the neural-latent correlation drops.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Figure 7g and 7j
outcomes.quote: At this point, several of these initial trends reverse; in particular, the total dimension begins to increase, whereas the correlation drops
outcomes.notes: Both readings hold in both areas. (a) Session 8 minus 4, PFC total dimension +0.936 and correlation -0.00764, CA1 +0.784 and -0.00603. (b) Mixed slopes over sessions 4 to 8, PFC +0.197 (P = 7.5e-07) and -0.00154 (P = 7e-05), CA1 +0.169 (P = 0.0022) and -0.00130 (P = 0.0022). The 19-unit CA1 variant gives the same signs.

outcomes.statement: Quadratic mixed-effects models of total dimension, neural-latent correlation and SNF over sessions have significant linear and quadratic terms in both PFC and CA1 (P < 10^-5), with the quadratic term opposite in sign to the linear term, so the effect of learning on these measures is non-monotonic.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Methods, Readout analysis, last paragraph; Supplementary Table 2 (not read)
outcomes.quote: We found strong, significant effects for both the linear and quadratic terms in PFC and CA1 for the total dimension, correlation and SNF ( P < 10 −5 ; Supplementary Table 2 ). In each case, the sign of the quadratic term was the opposite of the linear term

statistics.test: quadratic regression with mixed-effect intercepts, linear and quadratic terms
statistics.n: 8 rats, 8 sessions, per area and measure

outcomes.notes: All 12 P values below 1e-5, the largest 7.2e-07 raw (CA1 SNF quadratic term) and 1.2e-06 adjusted, with opposite signs in all six models (PFC dimension gamma -0.592, eta 0.0788; the paper's table gives -0.574 and 0.0765). The same holds with sessions coded 1 to 8 and with 19 CA1 units.

outcomes.statement: The quadratic mixed-effects model gives no evidence for a non-monotonic trend in SSF in either PFC or CA1 (P > 0.05).
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Supplementary Table 2 (not read)
outcomes.quote: We did not find evidence for a non-monotonic trend in the SSF in either region ( P > 0.05)

statistics.test: quadratic regression with mixed-effect intercepts, quadratic term

outcomes.notes: Quadratic term of the SSF model, PFC eta -0.00115 (P = 0.366, adjusted 0.382), CA1 eta 0.00121 (P = 0.313, adjusted 0.342); 19 CA1 units give P = 0.419.

outcomes.statement: The quadratic mixed-effects model has weaker but significant effects for the task-relevant dimension (P < 0.01), though it fits this quantity comparatively poorly in PFC.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Supplementary Fig. 12 and Table 2 (not read)
outcomes.quote: Although we did find weaker significant effects of the quadratic model for the task-relevant dimension ( P < 0.01), the model was a comparatively poorer fit to this quantity in PFC
outcomes.notes: PFC gamma 0.714 (P = 7.9e-06) and eta -0.0664 (P = 0.0025); CA1 gamma 1.01 (P = 5.5e-11) and eta -0.109 (P = 2.3e-07); all below 0.01 raw and adjusted. The paper's table gives PFC 0.716 and -0.0662, CA1 0.997 and -0.108. The poorer fit in PFC is not judged.

outcomes.statement: Linear mixed-effects models show significant monotonic effects of learning on SSF (P < 10^-3) and on the task-relevant dimension (P < 10^-5) in both PFC and CA1.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 2; Supplementary Table 2 (not read)
outcomes.quote: which demonstrated significant, monotonic effects of learning on the SSF and task-relevant dimension across both regions ( P < 10 −3 SSF and P < 10 −5 task dimension; Supplementary Table 2 )
outcomes.notes: All four slopes are positive with P < 0.05. PFC SSF 0.0119 (P = 3.0e-06), PFC task dimension 0.249 (P = 1.2e-07) and CA1 task dimension 0.242 (P = 2.1e-06) meet their bounds; CA1 SSF 0.00787 has P = 0.00106 raw and 0.00134 adjusted, just above 1e-3. With the code's 19 CA1 units CA1 SSF has P = 0.00065 and the full criterion holds (the paper's table gives 0.00055 with 19 units), so the shortfall rests on the unit count of the Methods and on random subsets near the bound.

outcomes.statement: Once behavioural and readout errors plateau at session four, the dimensionality measures and SSF increase while the neural-latent correlation decreases, as predicted for optimal representations late in learning.
outcomes.source: Results, Geometry of spatial representations in prefrontal cortex and CA1 during learning, paragraph 3; Discussion, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: Once the readout and behavioral errors begin to plateau at session four, we find that the ensuing trends are consistent with our predictions for optimal representations ... the dimensionality measures and SSF increase over learning, whereas the neural–latent correlation decreases
outcomes.notes: PFC holds under both readings (session 8 minus 4, total dimension +0.936, task dimension +0.502, SSF +0.0472, correlation -0.00764; mixed slopes over sessions 4 to 8 of the same signs). In CA1 total dimension (+0.784), SSF (+0.0531) and correlation (-0.00603) follow the prediction but the task-relevant dimension falls (-0.126; slope -0.015, P = 0.82), so the criterion fails in CA1 under both readings and with 19 CA1 units. The task dimension is on 19-unit subsets, as the claims file's pipeline takes it. With the task dimension on 24-unit CA1 subsets it falls under reading (a) (-0.0259) and has a slope of +0.0130 (P = 0.86) under reading (b). Reading (b) tests the sign only, so it holds there, although the slope is close to flat: with 24-unit task dimension sets the claim would hold in CA1 under reading (b) and be reproduced. The outcome is judged on the claims file's 19 units. Whether the claims file should take the task dimension on 24 CA1 units, as the Methods give for the geometric terms, is asked of a reader (questions/wakhloo-2026.yaml). The behavioural plateau it depends on (fig7d-behavioral-error-learning) is reproduced.

outcomes.statement: The Poisson GLMs reach an average cross-validated population D2 of 0.29 in PFC and 0.25 in CA1, with a standard deviation across rats of the session-averaged D2 of 0.022 in PFC and 0.1 in CA1.
outcomes.source: Methods, Generalized linear model analysis, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: The average cross-validated population D 2 across all sessions and rats was 0.29 in PFC and 0.25 in CA1, and the standard deviation of the session-averaged population D 2 across rats was 0.022 in PFC and 0.1 in CA1
outcomes.notes: Under the first reading (each unit's own best score, ddof 0) the mean population D2 is 0.279 in PFC and 0.245 in CA1, both within tolerance, and the standard deviation over rats of the session-averaged D2 is 0.1005 in CA1 (ddof 1 0.1075), within tolerance. In PFC it is 0.0599 (ddof 0) or 0.0640 (ddof 1) against 0.022 +- 0.0022, and no reading brings it within tolerance (0.057 to 0.066); the per-rat PFC means run from 0.161 (KL8) to 0.336 (ZT2). Counting units replaced by the null model as 0 gives PFC 0.301 and CA1 0.277 (outside). One PFC unit (JS21, one session) has no valid score, so that session's mean is nan as in the code and the mean over sessions skips it; the nan-mean over units gives 0.281. The chosen penalty is at an end of the grid for 1202 of 2327 PFC and 1750 of 3357 CA1 units. Three of the four values match, so the claim holds in part. The paper's own GLM fits (results/glm_results), matched to this attempt's rats by their unit counts, which agree in all 64 sessions of both areas, give the same session D2 (largest difference 2.7e-10 in PFC and 1.8e-09 in CA1 in the final run, 9.3e-11 and 2.3e-09 in the run the verifier read) and the same spread over rats, 0.0599 and 0.0640 in PFC and 0.1005 and 0.1075 in CA1, so the PFC gap to 0.022 is not a difference of fitting. The s.e.m. over rats, not a reading of the criterion, is 0.0226 in PFC (near 0.022) and 0.0380 in CA1 (against 0.1), so no single reading gives all four reported values. The task-relevant dimension from the paper's predictions agrees with this attempt's (r = 0.9996 PFC, 0.9997 CA1). How the paper computed the spread of 0.022 is a question for its authors (findings).
deviations: The GLM basis is the code's chosen one; its grid search was not repeated (see fig7h-task-dimension-increases). The cross-validation folds are scikit-learn's unshuffled KFold, as GridSearchCV uses for a regressor, so they are fixed, not random as the criterion supposes.

findings.statement: Rat ZT2 is split over two files that both carry session_id "01" and the same subject, with different units (233 and 240). Nothing in the files or the dandiset says that they are two parts of one day, or their order; the paper's code supplies it. Their time ranges (206 to 14664 s and 14760 to 30586 s) are consistent with that order, and no spike train or position trace is repeated between them or across any files.

Position is sampled at 27.0 frames per second (ER1) and 32.3 to 33.1 in the other files, where the paper states 30 fps; sessions last 13.0 to 20.0 minutes (median 15.85; 36 of the 64 between 15.0 and 16.0), where the paper states about 20. JS15's timestamps run from 3605 to 90718 s, about 24 hours, in a dataset described as one day.

The Methods give a standard deviation across rats of the session-averaged population D2 of 0.022 in PFC, and the paper's code does not compute it. The paper's own GLM fits (results/glm_results at commit 9674a6c) give 0.0599 (ddof 0) or 0.0640 (ddof 1), with per-rat PFC means from 0.161 to 0.336, and this attempt's fits give the same; the CA1 value (0.1) is matched by both. The s.e.m. over rats is 0.0226 in PFC but 0.0380 in CA1. Question for the authors - how was the 0.022 computed, and over which units and sessions?

The Methods use 19 PFC and 24 CA1 units per subset; the paper's code (run-pfc-hp-analysis-rats.py) and its results files use 19 in both areas, with the 24 commented out. The fewest units kept in a session are 19 (PFC) and 24 (CA1), so either is possible. The choice moves the CA1 SSF slope across the 1e-3 bound (P = 0.00106 with 24, 0.00065 with 19).
The Results give R2 = 0.48 for CA1 behaviour against readout error and the Fig. 7 legend 0.49; the code prints 0.477.

The SVC comparison notebook (figures/SM-svm-comparison-fig.ipynb) loads an older results file (abstraction/results/<area>_results_nu_dt_0.5.npy) that is not in the repository, so the Supplementary Fig. 3 rat panels cannot be traced to the published results files.

entries.name: wakhloo-2026
entries.title: Geometry of PFC and CA1 spatial codes during W-track learning (Wakhloo, Slatton and Chung 2026)
entries.description: Tests the rat findings of Wakhloo, Slatton and Chung (2026) on dandiset 000978, which holds the spikes, position and trials of 8 rats learning a W-track alternation task over 8 sessions in one day. It computes the task-averaged readout error of position and velocity, its geometric terms and the GLM task-relevant dimension per rat and session, with the paper's mixed-effects models. The paper's theory, network simulations and macaque and pose analyses are not about this dataset.
